notes.front: What is a Departmental Operations Center (DOC)?
notes.back: An operations centre dedicated to a single department or agency, focused on internal agency incident management.
notes.explanation: DOCs are often linked to, or represented in, a combined agency EOC.
notes.example: Like a single department's own control room, separate from the whole jurisdiction's EOC.

notes.front: What is an ICS or ICS-like EOC structure?
notes.back: An EOC configured using the standard ICS organisational structure, exactly or with slight modifications.
notes.explanation: This structure is familiar and aligns with the on-scene incident organisation.
notes.example: Like running the EOC with the same section names as the field team, so everyone recognises the layout.

notes.front: What is the Incident Support Model (ISM) EOC structure?
notes.back: An EOC structure that separates situational awareness from planning, and combines operations and logistics into incident support.
notes.explanation: It puts the EOC director in direct contact with situational awareness staff and streamlines resource sourcing.
notes.example: Like reorganising a team around information flow and resource support instead of copying the field's section names.

notes.front: What is the Departmental EOC structure?
notes.back: An EOC that uses day-to-day departmental/agency structure and relationships so representatives can function with minimal startup time.
notes.explanation: This is the third of the three common EOC team structures NIMS describes.
notes.example: Like each department showing up and working exactly as it does on a normal day.

notes.front: What is one primary function an EOC generally performs?
notes.back: Collecting, analysing and sharing information.
notes.explanation: EOCs are off-site locations where staff from multiple agencies support on-scene incident command.

notes.front: Which primary EOC function involves allocating and tracking resources?
notes.back: Supporting resource needs and requests, including allocation and tracking.
notes.explanation: This is one of the primary functions common to EOCs.

notes.front: Which primary EOC function involves coordinating plans and identifying future needs?
notes.back: Coordinating plans and determining current and future needs.
notes.explanation: This is one of the primary functions common to EOCs.

notes.front: Which less-universal EOC function involves providing policy direction?
notes.back: In some cases, providing coordination and policy direction.
notes.explanation: This is the least universal of the four EOC primary functions listed.

notes.front: What is the difference between what ICS does and what an EOC does?
notes.back: ICS manages on-scene, tactical-level response; EOCs are off-site and provide coordinated support to incident command.
notes.explanation: Learners often assume EOCs run tactics; they instead support the on-scene command from a distance.
notes.contrast: ICS is on scene and tactical; the EOC is off site and supporting.

notes.front: What physical forms can an EOC take?
notes.back: Fixed locations, temporary facilities, or virtual structures with staff participating remotely.
notes.explanation: EOCs are multidisciplinary, unlike operations centers run by a single organisation; an EOC need not be a building, as staff can take part remotely.
notes.source: IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 5, Visual 2, Note

notes.front: NIMS identifies three common ways of organising EOC teams: {{c1::ICS or ICS-like structure, Incident Support Model structure, and Departmental structure}}.
notes.explanation: Like ICS, EOCs use the NIMS management characteristic of modular organisation.

image.alt: Three EOC organisational structures side by side: the ICS or ICS-like structure (Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Admin.), the Incident Support Model (Situational Awareness, Planning Support, Resources Support, Center Support), and the Departmental structure (each agency in its own section).
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NIMS 2017, Figs. 7-9, pp. 47-48

notes.front: What is one of the four ISM EOC sections?
notes.back: The Situational Awareness Section.
notes.explanation: ISM separates this function from planning, unlike the ICS-like structure.

notes.front: Which ISM section works on future planning and coordinating requirements?
notes.back: The Planning Support Section.
notes.explanation: It is one of the four sections in the Incident Support Model structure.

notes.front: Which ISM section streamlines resource sourcing, ordering and tracking?
notes.back: The Resources Support Section.
notes.explanation: This section streamlines resource sourcing, ordering and tracking in the ISM structure.

notes.front: Which ISM section keeps the EOC facility and its staff supplied?
notes.back: The Center Support Section.
notes.explanation: It is the fourth section in the Incident Support Model structure.

notes.front: What are two factors that EOC organisation varies with?
notes.back: Any two of: authorities, staffing, agencies represented, facilities, communications, political considerations, the mission.
notes.explanation: This is why EOC teams vary widely between jurisdictions.

notes.front: What is one circumstance that might trigger EOC activation?
notes.back: More than one jurisdiction or agency becomes involved in an incident.
notes.explanation: This is one of several circumstances that can trigger an EOC to activate.

notes.front: Which EOC activation trigger covers the IC/UC warning of rapid escalation or cascading effects?
notes.back: The Incident Commander or Unified Command indicates the incident could expand rapidly, involve cascading effects, or require additional resources.
notes.explanation: This is one of several circumstances that can trigger an EOC to activate.

notes.front: Which EOC activation trigger is based on how a similar past incident was handled?
notes.back: A similar incident in the past led to EOC activation.
notes.explanation: This is one of several circumstances that can trigger an EOC to activate.

notes.front: Which EOC activation trigger is simply a direct order from the EOC director or an elected official?
notes.back: The EOC director, or an appointed or elected official, directs that the EOC be activated.
notes.explanation: This is one of several circumstances that can trigger an EOC to activate.

notes.front: Which EOC activation trigger covers a forecast hurricane or other imminent hazard?
notes.back: An incident is imminent, such as a predicted hurricane, flooding, hazardous weather, or elevated threat levels.
notes.explanation: This is one of several circumstances that can trigger an EOC to activate, before an incident even begins.

notes.front: Which EOC activation trigger is defined by thresholds written into the jurisdiction's emergency operations plan?
notes.back: Threshold events described in an emergency operations plan occur.
notes.explanation: This is one of several circumstances that can trigger an EOC to activate.

notes.front: Which EOC activation trigger covers anticipated significant impacts to the population?
notes.back: Significant impacts to the population are anticipated.
notes.explanation: This is the last of the listed circumstances that can trigger an EOC to activate.

notes.front: What does EOC Activation Level 3, Normal Operations/Steady State, mean?
notes.back: Normal activities for the EOC when no incident or specific risk has been identified; routine watch and warning.
notes.explanation: It is the lowest activation level, contrary to the intuition that a higher number means more activity.

notes.front: What does EOC Activation Level 2, Enhanced Steady-State/Partial Activation, mean?
notes.back: Certain EOC team members are activated to monitor a credible threat or to support a new, potentially evolving incident.
notes.explanation: It sits between normal operations and full activation.

notes.front: What does EOC Activation Level 1, Full Activation, mean?
notes.back: The EOC team, including personnel from all assisting agencies, is activated to support response to a major incident or credible threat.
notes.explanation: Level 1 is the highest activation level, even though it is numbered lowest.

notes.front: A jurisdiction is fully activating its EOC for a major hurricane. Which activation level number should it report using standard NIMS titles?
notes.back: Level 1, Full Activation.
notes.choices:
A) Level 1
B) Level 3
C) It depends on the hurricane's category
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: Level 3 is Normal Operations/Steady State, the lowest level, not full activation. C is wrong: the level reflects the EOC's state of activation, not the hazard's category directly.
notes.explanation: NIMS activation levels run backwards from what learners might expect: descending numbers mean higher activation, so full activation is Level 1.

notes.front: A jurisdiction runs its EOC with Operations, Planning, Logistics and Finance/Administration sections, just like its field ICS organisation, with 'Coordination' added to some titles. Which EOC structure is this?
notes.back: ICS or ICS-like EOC structure.
notes.explanation: This structure is chosen because it is familiar and aligns with the on-scene incident organisation.

notes.front: A jurisdiction's EOC has separate Situational Awareness and Planning Support sections, and merges operations and logistics into one Resources Support section. Which EOC structure is this?
notes.back: The Incident Support Model (ISM) structure.
notes.explanation: ISM separates situational awareness from planning and combines operations and logistics into incident support.

notes.front: A jurisdiction's EOC has each city department show up and coordinate exactly as they would on a normal working day, with minimal startup time. Which EOC structure is this?
notes.back: The Departmental structure.
notes.explanation: This structure uses day-to-day departmental relationships so representatives can function quickly with little preparation.

notes.front: A public works department runs its own internal coordination centre focused only on its own agency's incident response, separate from the jurisdiction's combined EOC. What is this called?
notes.back: A Departmental Operations Center (DOC).
notes.explanation: A DOC is dedicated to a single department, unlike a combined multiagency EOC.

notes.front: During a flood, on-scene teams are deploying sandbags under the Incident Commander, while a separate group elsewhere gathers resource requests from multiple agencies and coordinates support. Which group is the EOC?
notes.back: The off-site group coordinating resources and support across agencies.
notes.choices:
A) The off-site coordinating group
B) The on-scene sandbagging teams
C) The Incident Commander personally
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong because they describe the on-scene, tactical ICS response, not the off-site coordinating role an EOC plays.
notes.explanation: ICS manages on-scene tactical response; the EOC supports it from off site.

notes.front: A hurricane is forecast to make landfall in three days. Should the jurisdiction wait for it to make landfall before activating its EOC?
notes.back: No. An imminent incident, such as a predicted hurricane, is itself a listed trigger for EOC activation.
notes.choices:
A) No, activate now given the imminent threat
B) Yes, wait for landfall
C) Only if the National Guard has already been mobilised
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: EOC activation triggers include imminent incidents, not only ones that have already occurred. C is wrong: EOC activation is not conditioned on a specific other agency mobilising first.
notes.explanation: EOC activation triggers include incidents that are imminent, such as hurricane warnings.

notes.front: Two neighbouring jurisdictions run their EOCs very differently, because one has more partner agencies and different facilities than the other. What does NIMS say drives this variation?
notes.back: EOC organisation varies with factors such as authorities, staffing, agencies represented, facilities, communications, political considerations and the mission.
notes.explanation: This is why NIMS gives three example structures rather than mandating one.

notes.front: A credible tornado watch is issued for the area. The EOC director activates only the weather-monitoring and public-warning staff, not the whole team. What activation level is this?
notes.back: Level 2, Enhanced Steady-State/Partial Activation.
notes.choices:
A) Level 2
B) Level 1
C) Level 3
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: Level 1 is full activation of the whole team, not a partial one. C is wrong: Level 3 is normal operations with no credible threat identified.
notes.explanation: Level 2 activates certain team members to monitor a credible threat or support a new, evolving incident.

notes.front: A jurisdiction wants its EOC layout to feel immediately familiar to field responders who already know the ICS chart. Which of the three EOC structures best fits that goal?
notes.back: The ICS or ICS-like structure, since it aligns with the on-scene incident organisation.
notes.choices:
A) ICS or ICS-like structure
B) Incident Support Model structure
C) Departmental structure
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: ISM is chosen to streamline information and resource support, not for field familiarity. C is wrong: the Departmental structure mirrors day-to-day agency relationships, not the ICS chart.
notes.explanation: Each of the three EOC structures suits a different priority; familiarity with ICS favours the ICS or ICS-like structure.

notes.front: An incident no longer needs EOC support, and its functions can now be handled by individual organisations. What should the EOC director do?
notes.back: Deactivate EOC staff, returning the EOC to its normal operations/steady state, after completing resource demobilization.
notes.explanation: EOC leadership may phase deactivation, and planners normally include after-action review as part of it.

notes.front: Staff in an activated EOC spend the morning gathering field reports, tracking a shortage of generators, and drafting the next operational period's plan. Which primary EOC functions are they carrying out?
notes.back: Collecting and sharing information, supporting resource needs, and coordinating plans — three of the EOC's primary functions.
notes.explanation: These are the general functions NIMS lists for EOCs, distinct from the on-scene tactical work of ICS.

notes.front: An EOC organised under the Incident Support Model has one team tracking current conditions, another preparing resource requests, and another keeping the facility running. Which ISM sections are at work here?
notes.back: Situational Awareness, Resources Support, and Center Support — three of the model's four sections.
notes.explanation: ISM organises an EOC around these functions, rather than borrowing the ICS structure a field incident uses.
